utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are continuing with examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Delic. I would like to ask you some questions about your final piece of testimony yesterday. You mentioned a place called Zasavica, and you said you had your bags packed and ready to be taken. Where is Zasavica and what exactly was it? Was it a detention camp?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zasavica is a village near Bosanski Samac. It was mostly inhabited by Croats. It also bordered with some Serb villages. But it was also in the direction of the Crkvina Samac road. So this is where the road turned off to Zasavica. It was a right turning on that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you testified that people were being taken there to be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Who was being taken for detention there?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly Croats and Muslims were being detained, women and children, sometimes entire families. Mostly non-Serb citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know yourself of people who were taken and held in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that Muftic Jasna, with her child, was taken from her house. She was among the first. Sultanija Abramovic. Later in this period in September, this occurred more frequently, and more people were being taken away, so that all those who had somebody who was detained in the camp in Samac, the family members, were simply gathered up from their homes and deported to Zasavica. For example, Filduza Nalic was also taken away. I'm speaking about people who I know personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And when they were put in this village, were they put in -- or do you have any information as to where they were detained there or the conditions of their detention in the village?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions there and what was going on there is something that I know about from talking with those people. They were accommodated in the houses of people who used to live there before, Croats. A considerable number of the population who lived there before had already been deported in various exchanges, or they were expelled from their homes, so that new people were constantly being moved into these family houses in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were the people who were taken to Zasavica free to leave if they wanted?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that I knew told me that they couldn't leave the village simply. It was being monitored. They were also obliged to carry out work duties. I don't know whether you could call this compulsory labour or forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I turn now to the morning of the 4th of September. And you had received instructions to go to the courtyard of the school, you said. Did you go to the school on the 4th of September?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I went there in the morning before 8.00 a.m. Our house was nearby. Some of the neighbours who were not about to be exchanged, non-Serbs, my neighbours, they accompanied me, they helped me carry the bags that we had packed. They went with me to the schoolyard of the primary school. In the schoolyard, I found a large number of people, a crowd. Some were ready to leave and others were there to see off members of their families who were supposed to be leaving town.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: In this large crowd, were there -- what was the ethnicity of the people?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised mostly my neighbours, my Croat and Muslim neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were the people combatants, military persons, or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all civilians: women, children, the elderly. Also there were some younger people, but they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said the crowd was large. Could you give us some estimation as to how many people were there.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 200 people at least in that crowd. Not all of them went for the exchange, but at that point, that was how many people there were in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened next after you gathered in the yard.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out then that the primary school building in some hall or corridor, there was also a group of prisoners who were supposed to leave in that exchange as well. My husband was among them, and they told me that I could go inside, into the premises of the primary school, to see him, to see him for the first time after so many months and to actually speak to him freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you go and see your husband?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went up there with my children, and I saw him in a group with a few others who were supposed to be exchanged that morning. They were ready for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place exactly?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just one section of the corridor, and the people who were there were brought there that morning, and they were waiting for 8.00 when the roll call was supposed to start and when people were supposed to start getting onto the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What was the condition of your husband? What did he look like, for example, when you met him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed something that was very easy to notice: His head was shaved, and he looked much neater like that, compared to earlier occasions when I managed to see him when he had very long, dirty hair and also an unkempt beard. The others also had shaved heads. He also had a shaved head, and he was neatly shaved. He was wearing a jacket that he had had from before. His eyes were sunken. His face looked tortured. He was very emaciated. He was much thinner than when he left home on the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you see his teeth?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He attempted to smile, but he was trying to conceal that. And I tried to hide my astonishment because of the way he looked. He had always taken care of himself, and he had taken proper care of his teeth. But at that point, I noticed that a lot of teeth were missing, that he had gaps in places where he once had teeth.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court what happened after you spoke with your husband.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could hear the voices of the people from outside much louder now, and then we were told that we should be going up to the buses. My name was called out. They knew that I was coming with two children, so we were able to get onto the bus among the first. Then the other civilians were called out from the crowd. They quietly entered the buses. They were -- and we were handing our bags over to be placed in the luggage compartment. I had brought a bag for my husband as well, because we thought that each person would have the right to carry one bag. And since he didn't have anything, we brought a bag from home.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your husband get on the same bus as you and the children?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was called out later from a different list, and these people got onto the same bus. The prisoners, Dragan included, got onto the bus where we were, so we were able to sit together with our children.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How many buses in total were filled in this manner at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three buses ready at that point, and they were used for that particular exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know the person who called out your names, who was reading the names off the list?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the members of the Serbian Red Cross was on the bus. He used to work as a teacher before. So he was on the bus. And I know now that he was one of the people who was calling out the names. He called out my name, and we went into the bus. His name was Stevo Vasovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Tadic at the primary school that morning?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic joined the exchange as well. He was in a special -- in separate car. He wasn't on the buses, but he was following the buses. He was accompanied by two people in police uniforms. He had lists of people who were permitted to take part in the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You say he joined the exchange. So he joined it after the buses had left the primary school, or he joined it in that car at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there as people were getting onto the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. So when the buses left the primary school, where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the schoolyard of the primary school, the buses went first in the direction of the police station. Then several people were brought out of the police station in Samac who also got onto the buses, and they were also exchanged. I didn't know these people. They were from the nearby villages, as I found out later. After this short break, the bus went in the direction of Zasavica, and then a group of people who used to live in Bosanski Samac also got onto the buses, so they were in Zasavica at that time. And they also participated in this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did anybody who joined you either in the police station or in Zasavica wear a military uniform, or to the best of your knowledge, were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all civilians: Women, children, men. They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, what was the ethnic background of the people who joined the exchange?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People that I knew from the town were Muslims and Croats. But I could also tell from the clothes that the women were wearing, I could tell that the women -- some women came from Croat villages, and they were wearing their full costumes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. After you took -- collected some more people in Zasavica, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went on further towards Modrica. On the road, we were joined by several people from Modrica, also non-Serbs, because we inquired where they were from. The bus and the other buses were getting more and more full. Then we continued our journey through Doboj, Podnovlje, then Prnjavor, Bosanska Gradiska, and we were supposed to reach Dragalici, which was supposed to be the place of exchange. The journey lasted from 8.00 in the morning. We were in Bosanska Gradiska sometime after noon. I think it was 12.00 or 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did the bus stop then in Bosanska Gradiska, or did you continue on through Dragalici?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus stopped there because they told us that there were some slight problems because somebody was perhaps not being careful enough in their conversation, because we had heard that the number of people who were supposed to cross the bridge over the Sava does not correspond with the number of people that were supposed to be there in that exchange. Then there were people joining the convoy who were from other places, in Krajina and other places. In any case, we stopped at that place and we spent several hours there, until this problem was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: From whom were you getting the information that there was a problem with numbers?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they discussed this normally, the people who were accompanying the bus, the people from the Serbian Red Cross, and that's how we accidentally found out what the whole thing was about. Nobody actually explained this to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened after this problem was resolved.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, we continued on our way. We crossed the bridge over the Sava and passed into the so-called pink zone, where we encountered UN soldiers. We continued our journey, and I know that these soldiers were there at the ramp across the bridge. The road led towards Dragalici and continued on towards Slavonski Brod, in that direction. We continued our trip without stopping all the way until Dragalici. It was an abandoned and destroyed petrol station, a kind of resting area, a resting area along the highway.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buses stopped. They were parked one next to the other. We were permitted to get off the buses. The roll call was carried out again. Those who were called out, or a group of people which was called out, was permitted to leave that place. At the same time, we could see that there were buses on the opposite side full of people who were also coming out and crossing to the other side towards us in groups, and we were going in their direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage could I ask the witness to be shown two documents which I would like to actually tender into evidence. They are lists of exchanges from this day, and the witness's name appears on both lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Defence counsel have been provided already with these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, one of these lists is in fact already in evidence as Exhibit D4/3. But on that particular version, the -- there is a marking on the -- this witness's name, and so it's not legible. So I'd propose just to provide this copy of the list and -- where the witness's name is visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So a copy of D4/3 which is much better, which is clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It seems that on the other copy someone took a blue highlighter or something to the witness's name, and when it got photocopied, it didn't -- you can't read it. So this is one without that highlighting, so the witness's name is clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. So maybe we can look at D4/3 as well when we are looking at this cleaner copy, so that we just make sure it is one in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'll deal maybe first then with the list which is the same as Exhibit D4/3, and that is a list entitled, "Prisoners exchanged on the 4th of September, 1992 in Dragalic." And could I ask if the usher could put a B/C/S version on the ELMO for the defendants.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, D4/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because this document -- yes, it's maybe a confusing matter, but maybe I misunderstood the transcript. This is the line 15, and my learned friend is actually -- Ms. Reidy told us that it's Exhibit D4/3, and it's a list entitled, "Prisoners exchanged on the 4th of September, 1992 in Dragalic." And the exact title of this document is -- it's a list of "Persons exchanged on 4th of September, 1992 in Dragalic." Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is the title of D4/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the document in B/C/S version which is now on ELMO. So maybe it's rather confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm corrected. Mr. Pantelic is correct. It should be "Persons exchanged on the 4th of September in Dragalic," and not "prisoners exchanged." And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the translation is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll get that rectified. Because the translation of the -- the translation which exists with -- well, which is P4/3 where the witness's name is crossed out, has the correct title on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's get this sorted out. D4/3 has got the English translation already.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And that says, "List of persons."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: "List of persons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So then we do away with this one which -- the copy. The other translation which has a wrong title, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The only problem then is when you look at D4/3, beside number "1," where the witness's name is, in the translation -- in the English version it will say "crossed out," because that's what it looked like on D4/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can I look at D4/3, the English translation of D4/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Reidy, and also to the Defence counsel, I wanted us to agree that we take D4/3, the one which says, "List of persons exchanged on 4 September, 1992 in Dragalic," if we all agree that it's actually one and the same list and use that one for purposes of the evidence of this witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have these two copies to look at and compare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. D4/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just briefly consult with my client, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence is able to confirm this and agrees to this being admitted as evidence, with the proviso that on document marked D4/3, the name of Delic, Snjezana is clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that agreeable? Ms. Reidy?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite happy to use D4/3. But I'm just wondering how we addressed the problem that on D4/3, it's currently on the record, the first name is recorded as being crossed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought it was a machine smudge when taking the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, my understanding is it wasn't so much a smudge but a highlighter that -- in the photocopy. But D4/3, that being the English version, actually says at point 1, "crossed out." And that's actually my concern. Because if that's the record, then it's going to be difficult to ask the witness to identify this name. I have to apologise to the Court, I'm completely at fault about the second translation not being correct and I'm sorry it's causing inconvenience. Maybe it will be easier to work on the basis -- I'm happy to agree that it should be "persons exchanged," not "prisoners." And I will get that amended and have it filed with the Chamber as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So we do not accept this translation for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And we'll just deal with the Serbo-Croat copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we should have -- it should have its own number.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because in case of any matter arising, then all the copies will be there for whoever is looking at the evidence to check.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P51. And the previous exhibit that says "list of women to be exchanged," is P50, and that is under seal? Did you want that under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: No, there's no need to have it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, there seems to be a bit of confusion in the transcript, because all the way down this document is being called D4/3. And now it's P -- whatever the number that was just given. Could I clarify. Is this a "D" or a "P" document?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The two new documents I've handed up are now "P" documents. There is already a "D" document on file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So what the Prosecution will do is we'll get a correct translation of D -- of P51.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. So that we're now dealing with P51 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't ask the Defence about -- okay. Maybe I'll ask them when you deal with P50 whether they have any objection. All right. You can proceed with P51 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honours. In line 3 of page of 14, the Registrar said, Your Honours, the number will be P51, and now my learned colleague says it's P51 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because it's in Serbo-Croat, that's all. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. When the correct translation comes on the scene, then it will be P51.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is it possible to put P51 ter on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, is that your name at the top of that list?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's my name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at the bottom of that document. And you see the name Mijo Matanovic. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. We don't have the whole document on our screens. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. You can't see the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Usher can help us with zooming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. It will be moved appropriately so we can all have a view.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, can you now see the name Mijo Matanovic at the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, yes. I didn't know Mijo Matanovic before that exchange. I met him at the exchange because he shook hands with everyone who was set to leave and who was coming in through that exchange. As I said, I hadn't known him before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was he working for the authorities you were leaving, or was he working for the authorities in the place that you went to following the exchange?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, he was in the employ of the authorities who were taking care of the departure of citizens of Bosanski Samac who were not of Serb ethnicity. This modality was the only way for them to leave Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was he working in Samac, or was he working in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The document shows a list of 21 persons. Do you know some of the other people on that list?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I recall my former fellow citizens. I recognise the name of Mesic. It's Mesic in the English translation, but it's actually Mesic, followed by Stanic, Marija, a retired teacher.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It would be helpful for us maybe if you also mentioned the number, just the numbers of the list of the people that -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2 is Evica Mesic, whom I also now from around town. Number 3 is Marija Stanic. Number 4, Ridvana Mujkanovic, marked with -- her name is marked with plus 2, which means she had two children with her. Number 20 is Anica Nikolic, and number 21, Sultanija Abramovic. Those are the persons whom I knew personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Although there's 21 people on this list, were you exchanged with just the people on that list, or were you exchanged with a lot more people?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With more people. Those other persons could have even lived in Samac or in the surrounding villages. I'm not sure about that. But at any rate, the truck was full -- the bus was full.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask the witness now to be shown P50 ter, and if P50 ter could be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, while that's happening, I wonder whether you could clarify with the witness, at the bottom of the document, in the English translation, it says President of the commission for the exchange of prisoners and arrested civilians." I'd like to know from the witness whether she had ever been arrested as -- and/or was ever a prisoner to be therefore on this list designated as either of those two categories.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, would you answer Her Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I would qualify my status at the time. I was living at home, but my movement was restricted. I could not simply leave Bosanski Samac; that was not possible, because the entire town was in a blockade, was strictly controlled. At least, that's how it appeared to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: All I was going to say -- clearly, I understand that the English translation that I read from is the one that we have not admitted because of the -- the incorrect language in the title, as pointed out by Mr. Pantelic. But therefore, could I ask with respect to the question which you've just answered, with reference to the B/C/S version which is on the ELMO, being that I can't read B/C/S, I have to assume that it says the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, I think we can have that corrected -- dealt with, if we can have a copy given to the translators.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I believe the translators have a copy in their booths. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. So they can assist us --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I would only note that it appears to me that both translations, the translation which is D4/3, also uses the term "president for the commission for the exchange of prisoners," and it says "captured," as opposed to "arrested."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what are you saying? Is the English translation correct at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to attend it would appear so, because if you look at D4/3, you get the same translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why don't we ask the people who can translate, in the booth? Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would like to be of assistance to this Trial Chamber and also to my colleagues. In fact, Mr. Mijo Matanovic is a Croatian official, and it's not possible to translate because it's on Croatian language. And you have in English language practically one term. But in fact, I think that Her Honour Judge Williams, may be a little bit confused. It is not the commission of Samac municipality. Actually, Mr. Matanovic is an official from Croatian side, and this is a title of Croatian commission, in fact. Just for clarification. I don't want to spend so much time and have cross-examination. I mean, you can understand my position. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. And can we just have the interpreters deal with that, on P51 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So basically, Mr. Pantelic, this list means list of persons in respect of a completed exchange, and it's issued by the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That is the conclusion. That is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And that is their document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To the other side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Would you like the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And just one second. This word "prisoners," again, is that accurate? Prisoners? Is it "prisoners," or "person," or you don't know, in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The title of Croatian commission is -- well, the signature is Mr. Mijo Matanovic, president of commission for exchanged prisoners and captured or arrested civilians. That is the official title of Croatian commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah. We will simply wait for the English translation of P51 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. Counsel cannot translate for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I think when you put in these documents, just put them in one by one in an orderly fashion and explain what the document is, because by just putting all these documents at one go, four, five, six, there's a lot of confusion and a waste of your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we are now dealing with P50?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I thought we were going to finish P51 ter and just have the witness read out the name of the commission in B/C/S so that it would be translated. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah, you can complete that. I think the best way is just to wait for the translation of P51 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But you can complete your questions on P51 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say wait for the written translation, you mean not an oral translation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Look, this witness was just one of the people who was exchanged. I don't think she's competent to tell us who Mijo Matanovic was. She had already said she didn't know him. She met him on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Your Honour. That's why I -- you know, I didn't get into the testimony which Mr. Pantelic gave. I simply wanted to clarify if you would like a translation of the title -- of his title now orally from the translators here in the booth or whether, when you speak about translation, you mean waiting for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. We shall wait for the whole document P51 ter to be translated into English, and that's the one we shall rely upon. Definitely, counsel can't translate for us. That's the normal way of our procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As far as I'm concerned, that's finished with P51 ter, and I will ask the witness to have a look at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. P50 ter. And could I ask the usher if he could place P50 ter on the ELMO. Could I ask you to please move the document up a little bit so we could see the stamp at the bottom. Your Honour, just at the bottom, if you want to know, is a document with a Serbia Red Cross stamp, and the Prosecution's position is that this was the list prepared on the Serbian side for the exchange within which this witness was involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to object. There is no stamp of the Serbian Red Cross on this document. That's not what's written on the stamp, unlike what Ms. Reidy says. What it says on the stamp is just "Red Cross," not "Serbian Red Cross."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. And I just wanted to make out that this is from the Serbian authorities and not from the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you look at the English translation, P50, it says, "stamp of Bosanski Samac Red Cross," and then "signature." That's what the English translation says. And we take that as the correct translation. If the Defence are disputing that, then they can say -- they can place their stand on the record, and then during the Defence case, they can call witnesses, yes, to discuss the stamp or any other matter surrounding the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will raise this issue during the cross-examination of this witness. We just wanted to avoid the record including that this is a document marked by a stamp of the Serbian Red Cross. It can be introduced as a document issued by the Bosanski Samac Red Cross. Moreover, the organisation of the Red Cross is not an authority. It's a humanitarian organisation designed to help civilians. That is the essence, the main point of our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Reidy, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, can you confirm for us whether your name also appears on this list.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Number 1 is Snjezana Delic, marked with plus 2, meaning with two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at names at numbers 5 and number 6 on that list. Do you know those two names of those two people?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Numbers 5 and 6 are persons I know, Marta and Azra Vuco, both from Bosanski Samac. They are interrelated. Azra Vuco is the daughter-in-law of Marta Vuco.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnic background of these two women?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marta Vuco is a Croat, and Azra comes from a Muslim family and married Marta's son. I don't know how she declared herself at that time, but she was originally a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, did these two women -- do you know for a fact if they were exchanged with you on that day on the 4th of September?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were both exchanged that day, together with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you confirm from that list that -- anyone you recognise on that list, that these were all women and they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What are you asking the witness to do? To confirm from that anyone you recognise on the list --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see, the people she recognised.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Who she recognised, exactly.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides the people that I already mentioned, at the end of the list, under number 27, it's Anica Nikolic, and the name under 28, Sultanija Abramovic. I knew those two people as well. All the mentioned persons were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And I take it they were all women as well, were they?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, just for the record, there is a different number of people on the list you're looking at now compared to the other list which said -- which only had 21. Would you have any information as to why there's a difference in numbers?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't receive any explanation about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask, did you see this list that you have in front of you at any stage on the 4th of September when you left Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I personally didn't see a list. I never held one in my hand. My name was called out, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I've finished with the document, if the Bench have any questions, or else I'll ask the usher to remove it from the ELMO. Thank you. I'm finished with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, they can be removed. I just want to make it clear that P50 ter and P50 have been admitted into evidence with the objections of the Defence, as explained by Mr. Krgovic, noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, on -- at the time of your exchange, were you given any documentation with respect to the property you had left behind you in Bosanski Samac, the things you couldn't fit into the bags you had?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive any documents. Everything stayed the way it was on that last day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you given any explanation about what would happen to everything that you had to leave behind you in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive an explanation, but I must say that I didn't ask for one either. We had this opportunity to get out, and we didn't want to disrupt it by asking any questions or by being wise guys, if I can put it that way, or to ask for something that was not possible for us to get at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At any stage prior to that, when you had gone to check in at the Red Cross, were you ever told by Mr. Tadic or any other person there what would be the fate of your property?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't find anything out. I wasn't told anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, do you have any family left in Bosanski Samac now?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any family in Bosanski Samac. My mother lived in Bosanski Samac until 1995. She's living with me now. She left Bosanski Samac. My brother no longer lives in Bosanski Samac either, and I don't have any other family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was your brother -- did your brother leave Bosanski Samac also in an exchange or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left with the help of friends. He left Samac earlier. He didn't get out through an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And why did your brother leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother lived alone in an apartment in Samac. At that time, that was already 1995. So it's several years after 1992, after we left Bosanski Samac. She was born in 1910, and she thought that she would stay there, live there for the rest of her days, remain in town. At that time, Serb citizens from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina were settling in Bosanski Samac, so that her apartment was required to house new refugees. She was told that she would be in the position where she would have to have her apartment -- she would have to make her apartment available for the use of refugees, and therefore, we managed to get my mother out of Bosanski Samac with the help of a few friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can I just consult with my colleague for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's the end of the Prosecution examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just would like to ask the Chamber to make it possible to have a break now so that we could consult -- I could consult my client about this part of the testimony concerning the exchange. Some topics have been mentioned which I haven't had an opportunity to consult about with my client, so I'm wondering if it would be possible to have the break now, instead of in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: You know, maybe I can help here, Your Honour. If you want to use the next 15 minutes, I have only one line of questioning, and I can probably finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you want to cross-examine. You can start.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I can probably fill five or ten minutes until the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Yes, you can go ahead. Mr. Krgovic, if you want to speak with your client as the

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do that during the break, because I think that the cross-examination by Ms. Baen will take -- take up the time until the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I guess we'll find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Delic. My name is Catharine Baen, and I'm one of the lawyers for Milan Simic. And I actually just have one area I'd like to cover with you, which is on the primary school. That's really what I want to focus on. Okay. So you testified today that you -- your husband was being held in the primary school; right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And you also mentioned earlier today that at some point, you were allowed to go in and visit your husband at the primary school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And this wasn't the only time that you actually had been allowed to go in to visit him; correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But I want to explain what is implied under the term "visit" in my case. I could see him very briefly, and I couldn't always talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to get to that. And in fact, I'm asking my questions from your statement that you gave to the OTP. So I'm going to give you a chance -- if I don't give you a chance to explain it, then I promise you Ms. Reidy will let you explain it. Okay? So we'd established that that wasn't the only time that you went in to visit your husband; right? In fact, you had been allowed to see him at one point, I think, on the average of once a week; right? The guards would allow you in once a week?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I would like to say that these visits were not permitted. It depended on the goodwill of a guard whom I knew. So at that point, on his own risk, he would let me see my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Exactly. And that's what I'm saying. But you didn't just walk in freely. Somebody had to allow you to go in. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go in. It was just a visit in front of the entrance to the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So you would go to the primary school, and one of the guards you knew would permit your husband to come to the front of the primary school, and you would visit him; correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And this happened, on the average, once a week for some period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. I can't confirm that exactly, but if we averaged out the number of visits and the time, yes, that was it, on average.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And this was because some of these guards you mentioned, they actually had been pupils of yours at the school at one point; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And these guards that we're talking about, they also allowed you to send food and to send some clean clothes to your husband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: How often did that happen? How often did you send food and clean clothes to your husband? How often were you allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're using a term here "once a week." If this is statistically the average then yes, we could work it out like that. But, in fact, I don't know whether it was three days in a row and then no visit for ten days because it wasn't possible to bring anything, and so on. So there is a difference there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I know. And I promise I'm not trying to hold you to any set number. I'm just trying to give the Trial Chamber a general idea of what was going on, that's all. So thank you for that. And at the primary school, there were also some - I think I'm using [Realtime transcript read in error "Yugoslavia"] your words, actually - "good guards," who allowed other prisoners to be visited by their families; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that, that they had contact with their relatives in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there needs to be a correction in the transcript. Page 29, line 8, it says "I think I'm Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I may have said that, but I don't remember saying that. I think what I said was "I'm using your words, actually," instead of "Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The audio people will correct it with the people who work on the transcripts finally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And we were talking about the good guards. You lived near the primary school at that time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And since you lived near the primary school, you were actually able to see and you knew who was guarding the prisoners; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could. Not always, but that was also how I found out who was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: You don't like the word "always," but quite often you were aware of who was guarding at the primary school; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these terms are so indefinite, and they give a stronger impression, but there is actually very little behind them. There is so little that one could have done on these visits, even with the good guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, I'm sorry to hold you down. I don't mean to quibble over words. And that's why so many people don't like lawyers is because we do that. But I'm just trying to get a general idea of what you could see and what you knew, and I promise you I'm not trying to trick you. Okay? So since you knew -- if you don't like the word "often," you knew at some point who was guarding the primary school, and I guess I'm assuming you knew when they were changing shifts, too. Sometimes you had that information, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I knew -- yes, this solution is a little more realistic. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. So based on your knowledge or based on the proximity of your house to the primary school and the times when you saw the guards changing shifts, could you get an idea of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could I just intervene, because I think it's not clear. The witness's answer was "sometimes I knew, yes. This solution is little more realistic." It's certainly my impression that she's saying that sometimes she knew. What exact meaning -- that's the frequency of time she knew. But it's not clear what that information was she knew. That she knew they were there? Who the guards were? Or specifically, as Ms. Baen had asked, about the changing shifts. And since Ms. Baen wishes to pursue this issue about changing guards, I think it's important to clarify whether the witness knew sometimes who the guards were or sometimes knew when the shifts or exactly what it was she knew sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: That's fine with me. She can explain -- that's fine with me. I'm headed that way, but we can clear that up right now, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, did you understand the Prosecutor, what she was wanting you to clarify?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly when the guards were changing. When I saw or found out that it was possible to take something, then I would use such an opportunity. And this happened occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Could you tell me generally when these shift changes took place. Were they in the middle of the afternoon? Were they late at night? Were they early in the morning? Just generally.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the shifts took place, the change of shifts took place. I couldn't always walk around, move around, and follow things like that. I couldn't even go up to the school, because that was sometimes very risky.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: But what I'm asking is, obviously, you waited until one of these guards you knew or these ex-pupils of yours would come on shift, because then you knew it was sometimes okay to go over there to maybe visit your husband. What I'm asking you, if you remember, is when this happened. Was this late at night when you went to visit your husband? Was it early in the morning? Was it in the middle of the afternoon? Do you remember when you went to go visit your husband?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to go in the mornings usually, around 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning, or in the afternoon at about 3.00 or 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. So -- okay. So it seems as though there were at least two to three shifts? Answer if you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- objection. Ms. Baen is now making --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- a leap of information which is simply not a true reflection of the record. Because I think the first question, the witness simply testified that she went -- she said either in the morning or the afternoon. She's not testified that she went at the times when guards were shifted or anything like that. And because the question -- the last question Ms. Baen posed was: Do you remember when you went to visit your husband? Ms. Baen is now trying to imply that she always went at the same time there was a shift change. And that's not what the witness testified. I think the record reflects that. You know, so -- so again, I think that the question of Ms. Baen's is misleading, and on that ground, I'd object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't think so, because the witness can answer if she knows, because she says -- the question is: So it seems as though there were at least two to three shifts? Answer if you know." If the witness doesn't know, she can say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know how the guards changed shifts. It wasn't something that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. The names -- what I'd like to know now is can you give me the names of these pupils who helped you -- ex-pupils who helped you at the primary school.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Where did you teach them?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were different generations during the course of 14 years of my work. Some of them had completed school earlier. And sometimes they were there once during one period. But in any case, I can't repeat their names. I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: How many of them were there who helped you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's two or three people together. Not all of them were my pupils. It was two or three guards, and then -- it was the guards and then two or three people who were there next to the guards who would say, "Well, you can let her go." I mean, they would say something simple like that to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So these two or three people who used to be students of yours who were helping you to see your husband as he was being held at the primary school, you don't remember anything about them. Is that what you're telling the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even try to remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: But all these pupils -- you never taught anywhere but Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So hypothetically, if I showed you a yearbook with all the students when you taught there, would you recognise these people who helped you at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I would. They have very similar names and surnames. There's different school generations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So you weren't -- these men were doing you a huge favour, it seems, and you don't remember anything about these men who did these huge favours for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I object. The witness has said she doesn't remember their names, not that she doesn't remember anything about them, as Ms. Baen is trying to put it. And this is the second time she's asked this question. I didn't object the first time but now she's exactly said, "you didn't remember anything about them," and the witness has clearly said she doesn't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't agree with the objection. I don't see anything wrong with pursuing the matter, as Ms. Baen is doing. Ms. Baen, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I do want to -- I don't want to intimidate this woman, and I feel like -- this is what I feel like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You can go ahead. The objection is overruled. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, I think you have told someone before that the reason -- or that actually, these guards that helped you, these ex-pupils that helped you, that they could have gotten in trouble -- it was your opinion that they really could have gotten in serious trouble if anybody found out that they were helping you. You've told someone that at some point, haven't you? Did you not ever tell the OTP that when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible to assume that they would not have been in a favourable position at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And it's really important that if there are some witnesses who might help any of our clients in this case, if we find out about them, that it's real important we find out who they are so that we are able to go talk to them, investigate, and see if they should come testify before the Trial Chamber, and that's why I'm asking these questions. So if you in fact -- I know you say you don't remember anything about these people who helped you. But if you in fact remember, there are things that we can do to protect these people's names. You don't have to say on the Internet or live in this courtroom what their names are. So bearing that in mind, is your -- is your answer still the same? You don't remember anything about these men whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I'm happy to let Ms. Baen pursue the matter about the memory of this witness and that and test in that sense a credibility issue, but she simply said she's doing this in order to investigate her client's case, not to question this witness on the testimony she's given here or to pursue matters, to find out if there's a witness for her client. She's taking instructions from her client. And I just think this is somehow inappropriate in cross-examination, where she's asking for the names for a purpose, it seems, beyond testing the testimony she's given here in court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me take it up. Witness, the point the Defence counsel is trying to get at is this: If you know the names of these persons who were helping you, who allowed you to see your husband during the time that he was in detention, but you feel that if you disclose their names, they may be in trouble with the authorities because that could be -- that conduct would be seen as betrayal on their part, you can have their names written on a piece of paper, and that piece of paper can be passed to the Defence counsel and the Prosecution counsel and to the Bench, and that piece of paper will not be produced on public records. It can be on the Trial Chamber's record, under seal. And the orders on documents which are under seal is that nobody should disclose the contents of those documents to anybody outside this courtroom without the authority of the Trial Chamber. So they can be protected. We've had those procedures, you know, done before in -- with regard to other witnesses and other persons, the names who have to be protected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could give several names of people who took part in this. Whether they were my pupils or not is probably something that can be established later. There is no need for me to protect them especially. These people didn't do anything bad by permitting a bag with two or three sandwiches or a bag with some fresh clothes to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. Maybe we can -- yes, we can take our break, as usual, and resume our proceedings at 16.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, we left off, and I believe you told the Trial Chamber or Judge Mumba, you said you could give several names of people who took part in this. Whether they were your pupils or not, to be established later. Okay. Do you want to go ahead and provide those names now? Would you do that for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could give you two names, for instance. At this moment, I recall the name -- last name only vaguely. The name is Misa, and he's the son of Pero Sargija from Samac, and the other man is -- and the last name of that man is Bogdanovic. And another person is Veselin Zugic. I also wish to point out that they did not always serve as guards on that spot, but they were able to help me. And I didn't know all the guards, but on those occasions, they helped me get some stuff inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. And these people, the names you just mentioned, were these the people who were your ex-students, or were these the other people who were guarding who were not your students?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Misa was a former student of mine. Veselin used to be a colleague of my husband's.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. And you just mentioned that sometimes these people were guards and at other times they weren't serving as guards but they helped you; right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had friends and acquaintances who had access to the guards. I don't know why they happened to be there on the spot, but they managed to put this bag of sandwiches into the guard's hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. You testified just a little bit ago before the break - page 33, line 22, for purposes of the record - "It's two or three people together. Not all of them were my pupils. It was two or three guards, and then it was the guards, and then two or three people who were there next to the guards who would say, 'Well, you can let her go. I mean, they would say something simple like that to them.'" Do you remember the names of any of these other people who helped -- these other people you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. I didn't even know those people. I can't remember their names. I must say that they all had the same kind of uniform, and at that time, I was not able to distinguish who was a guard and who was not. The only thing that mattered to me was which one of them displayed enough goodwill.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Of course. Okay. I'm almost done, but I have just a few more detailed questions about these people working at the primary school. These several people who helped you, some of the ones you mentioned, and these other ones who had uniforms on, when they helped you, was it always the same group together helping you, or were there different combinations of them there at different times?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were different people. I didn't know them. But I contacted the wives of other detainees who would sometimes tell me, "Give me your stuff, and I'll get it inside. I happen to know the guard." So those were just attempts with -- without any guarantee of success. It was not a regular transaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, maybe my question was just confusing. What I'm trying to get at is all the people you mentioned, your ex-students, and then these other people who worked as guards, all the people you mentioned who helped you see your husband or get food through to your husband or clothes through to your husband, did all those people who helped you, were they always working there together at the same time when you went to visit, or were they changed up different times you went to visit? Was it maybe one of that group of people you mentioned -- different combinations, is what I'm trying to find out. Or were they always the same people at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different people in different combinations. It was not one and the same group all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. One more thing. When you and I first started talking here, these "good guards" who helped the other families that you were talking about just a second ago, these were different guards from the ones who helped you, some of them, or were they all the same guards? In other words, were there some different guards who didn't help you who you learned helped these other families who went to the primary school?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't happen that way. You could either get something through or not, regardless of who was bringing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I must have asked another confusing question. What I'm trying to find out -- you mentioned all these people who helped you on different occasions. Earlier, you mentioned that there were some other families who were also helped at the primary school. Were these families helped by the same people who helped you, or were there some other guards who were different guards who helped those other families? Or if you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can give you a for-sure answer to that question. I can't say that the people who helped me didn't help others, or the other way around, that they were unwilling to help me and were able to do something for someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, let me try it one more time. When you talked to these other people who went to visit their families or were helped at the primary school, did they give you the names, or did you hear about -- from them, did you hear about other guards who had helped them at the school? In addition to the people who helped you, were there people who helped these other families?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can put it that way, too. If I may add to my previous answer an illustration of a successful contact of that kind: At one point, having spotted a good moment, I headed for the primary school, and I took the children with me on that day because I thought it might be possible for them to see their father. I don't know that guard. He's originally from one of the surrounding villages. But at that moment, I was allowed to approach the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Does this have to do with the names of the guards? I'm sorry to interrupt you. Does this have to do with the names of the guards? Okay. What was the name of the guard? I know about this in your statement, and we can go on and on about that, but right now what I want to know about is just the names of the guards. And I promise you, if you want to go on with this on direct examination, you can do that. But this is my last question, and I'm going to sit down and leave you alone. Is this a name of another guard that you didn't tell me about who helped you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, I'm talking about an attempt which was aborted because another person prevented it. But the guard in question had displayed his goodwill.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And what was that guard's name who showed the goodwill?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the guard, I don't know it. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you, Ms. Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. The next counsel. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Delic. My name is Dragan Krgovic. I'm an attorney at law. And I was appointed by this Court as Defence counsel for Mr. Tadic. Before starting my cross-examination, I wish to say something that I was authorised to say by my client, namely, that he is deeply sorry for all that you and your family, specifically your husband, your brother, and your sister-in-law, had to endure. He knows that you were his former colleague at school. He knew your brother-in-law, and he is -- he regrets everything you had to endure in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does that mean that he recognises that it was indeed so terrible, that it was real torture?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He only wishes to express his regret over everything that had happened.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement and in your testimony, you said that before the outbreak of the conflict in Bosanski Samac, there was a municipal conference of the Red Cross. That was the official name of the Red Cross organisation at the time which existed even before the outbreak of the conflict. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in November 1991, a large exchange took place in the territory of Bosanski Samac between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Red Cross of Bosanski Samac was involved in that exchange and in the later accommodation of people who had then arrived into the territory of Bosanski Samac, and in the departure of those who were leaving the place?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure we are speaking about the same event. Maybe I have something different in mind. But if we are talking about the same thing, what I know is that at one point in the secondary school building, namely in the gym, a large number of people was housed, people who had come from Vukovar, and were put up on the school premises for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The local population and the Red Cross organisation, I suppose, helped out in this endeavour?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I know that they would spend a certain number of hours there, and it would have been logical for people to participate in helping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that on the first day of the outbreak of the conflict in Bosanski Samac, bread and milk were distributed during the first days while the shops were closed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. During the first days, these products were distributed to people -- at least, the people who I knew, people from my street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this distribution was organised by neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how it was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all the citizens of Bosanski Samac profited from this distribution, regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I myself was able to get this bread and milk during the first two days. Those were the only two products that were distributed. Otherwise, I couldn't get hold of them in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that people who were of poor financial status received allowances or some sort of assistance in aid, in food?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your husband's father, Hasan Delic, received some sort of aid?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Bosanski Samac, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, the offices of the Red Cross were in the home for retired people.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The new building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have to wait a little for the interpreters so they can catch up. You and I speak the same language and understand each other very well. Outside that building, there was a flag of the Red Cross flying.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, but it would have been logical for it to be there. I don't know if it was there the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the ground floor, there were rooms where there were people dealing with the work obligation.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any such details. I don't know what happened on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And upstairs, there was the office where you would find Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this office where Miroslav Tadic sat belonged to the civilian defence and that Mr. Miroslav Tadic was employed by the civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mastic, Velimir -- Velimir Mastic was involved in the work of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I know this man --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to help you. He used to be the director of the centre for social work.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How about Anka Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew her, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Dusanka Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall at the moment. I can't recall that I knew her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: These people that you knew, did they first work in the centre for social work and then transfer to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anka Jovanovic and Velimir did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Husein Mustafic worked in the Red Cross of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really place that name at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How about Zijad Pelesevic, only if you know him.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any Zijad Pelesevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Bahrain -- Baknia Abdebegovic [phoen], did he work at Mebos?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I cannot recognise the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Suhra Porobic?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know she's in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was she involved with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I knew her as a worker of the Sit company.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name, the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness -- or is it counsel? The interpreter said they didn't hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Barjaktarevic, Husein.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Husein Barjaktarevic?
